sections.name: Part 1 · The Percentage Toolkit
sections.intro:
Welcome to your own audit, analyst.

There is no pass mark here. Nothing is being graded.

This decides what your next unit is made of — so an honest answer helps you more than a lucky one.

You can skip anything. A skip is useful information, not a failure. It tells me where to go next.

Start with your oldest tool: the gears.

parts.label: 10% of £80 (£)
parts._working: 10% means divide by 10: 80 ÷ 10 = £8. The 10% machine from board meeting 1.

parts.label: 5% of £80 (£)
parts._working: 5% is half of 10%: half of £8 = £4.

questions.prompt: A busier day. The stall takes £300.

parts.label: 1% of £300 (£)
parts._working: 1% is the 10% divided by 10 again: £30 ÷ 10 = £3.

questions.prompt: A quiet day. The stall takes £60.

parts.label: 25% of £60 (£)
parts._working: 25% is a quarter: halve £60 to £30, halve again to £15.

parts.label: 75% of £60 (£)
parts._working: 75% is three quarters: the quarter is £15, so 3 × £15 = £45. (Or £60 − £15.)

questions.prompt: Now build two awkward ones out of your gears, like Lego.

parts.label: 95% of £140 (£)
parts._working: The clever route is backwards: 95% is everything except 5%. 10% of £140 = £14, so 5% = £7, and £140 − £7 = £133. Building it forwards from 50 + 25 + 20 also works but takes longer — either way earns the mark.

sections.name: Part 2 · Reading a Sale Sign
sections.intro:
Shops spend millions on these signs.

You learned to read them like an analyst. Prove it.

questions.prompt: A coat is priced at £40. The sign says 25% off.

parts.label: Money off (£)
parts._working: 25% of £40 is a quarter: halve to £20, halve again to £10.

questions.prompt:
Another sign, the classic one.

It says WAS £80 — NOW £60.

parts.label: So what percentage off is that? (%)
parts._working: £20 out of the old price £80 = 20/80 = a quarter = 25%. The analyst's reverse move from board meeting 3. Both 25 and 0.25 are accepted because the engine reads a typed "25%" as 0.25 — without the twin, a correct answer written with a percent sign marks wrong.

questions.prompt:
Two shops, and the same coat in both. Each one is priced at £100 before any discount.

Shop A takes 30% off. Shop B takes £25 off.
 Price beforeThe offer
Shop A£10030% off
Shop B£100£25 off

parts.label: Shop A's price (£)
parts._working: 30% of £100 = £30 off, so £100 − £30 = £70. (Out of 100 the percentage IS the money.)

parts.label: Which shop is cheaper — A or B?
parts._working: Shop A, at £70 against £75. The bigger-sounding offer happens to be the better one here, which is not always true — s4 is where that bites.

questions.prompt:
A sneaky one. A game's sign says WAS £50 — NOW £40.

Above it, in big letters, the shop claims 25% OFF!

parts.label: The real discount (%)
parts._working: £10 off out of £50 = 10/50 = 1/5 = 20%. Decimal twin included for a typed "20%".

parts.label: Is the sign telling the truth? (yes/no)
parts._working: No. The real discount is 20%, and the sign claims 25% — it has flattered itself by five percentage points. This is the question that proves the whole of board meeting 3 landed.

sections.name: Part 3 · Profit, Properly
sections.intro:
Now the books.

Revenue is money in. Costs are money out. Profit is what is left.

These are fresh numbers, not the week you already did — so this checks the method, not your memory.

questions.prompt: Tuesday is awful. The stall takes £26 and spends £31.

parts.label: Tuesday's profit (£, use a minus sign)
parts._working: 26 − 31 = −5. A loss of £5. Money out was bigger than money in, so the answer drops below zero — Unit 1's negatives earning their keep.

questions.prompt:
Here is a whole fresh week, already worked out day by day.

Monday made £40. Tuesday lost £6. Wednesday made £25. Thursday made nothing at all. Friday made £51.
 MonTueWedThuFri
Profit that day£40−£6£25£0£51

parts.label: The whole week's profit, Monday to Friday (£)
parts._working: 40 − 6 + 25 + 0 + 51. Running total: 40, then 34, then 59, then 59, then £110. Tuesday's loss takes £6 away rather than adding it, which is the only trap in the question.

questions.prompt:
Saturday, and this one runs backwards.

You know the profit was £45. You know the costs were £38.

Nobody wrote down the takings.

parts.label: Saturday's revenue (£)
parts._working: Profit = revenue − costs, so revenue = profit + costs = 45 + 38 = £83. Check it forwards: 83 − 38 = 45 ✓.

parts.label: In one sentence, how did you work that out?
parts._working: HUMAN REVIEW — no accept list, so this renders as a textarea and marks as "review" whatever she writes. There is no wrong answer. What to look for: does she describe undoing the subtraction (adding the costs back on), or does she describe guessing and checking? Both get to £83, but they are different stages of understanding, and that difference decides how much scaffolding Unit 4 needs. A skip here is also informative.

sections.name: Part 4 · The Margin
sections.intro:
Last part, and the hardest.

A profit on its own tells you almost nothing. The margin is the number that judges it.

questions.prompt: You buy a box of trainers for £40. You sell them for £50.

parts.label: Margin (%)
parts._working: £10 profit compared with the £40 it cost: 10/40 = a quarter = 25%. Decimal twin for a typed "25%".

questions.prompt:
Two market stalls, and they made exactly the same profit.

Ana spends £50 and makes £10. Ben spends £200 and also makes £10.
 What they spendProfit
Ana£50£10
Ben£200£10

parts.label: Ben's margin (%)
parts._working: 10/200 = 1/20 = 5%. Gear check: 10% of £200 is £20, so £10 is half of that, 5%.

parts.label: Whose money is working harder — Ana or Ben?
parts._working: Ana. Same £10 of profit from a quarter of the money. Phrased as "working harder" rather than "better business" on purpose — it is the margin that is being asked about, not a verdict on the people.

questions.prompt:
Now the trap you have met before.

Business A spends £60 and runs a margin of 50%. Business B spends £400 and runs a margin of 10%.
 What it spendsMargin
Business A£6050%
Business B£40010%

parts.label: Which one puts more money in the till — A or B?
parts._working: Business B, at £40 against £30 — a fifth of A's margin and still more money, because it is working with far more cost. The margin judges a profit; it does not tell you the size of one.

questions.prompt:
Last question, analyst, and it is a judgement rather than a sum.

A small online bookshop lost £30 in its first year and lost £10 in its second year.

Its revenue was £100 in year 1 and £400 in year 2.
 Year 1Year 2
Revenue£100£400
Loss that year£30£10

parts.label: Both years added together, what is the total profit? (£, use a minus sign)
parts._working: A loss of £30 and a loss of £10: (−30) + (−10) = −£40. Two years of trading, £40 down.

parts.label: In one sentence — would you put your own money into it, and why?
parts._working: HUMAN REVIEW — no accept list, so it renders as a textarea and marks as "review". There is no right answer and both verdicts are defensible. What to look for: does she notice that the revenue QUADRUPLED while the loss SHRANK to a third? That pair is the Riverbend shape from board meeting 6, and spotting it unprompted is the single most advanced thing in this checkpoint. A "no" with a reason about the losses is still a good answer; a "yes" that cites the growth is better; noticing both directions is best of all. A skip tells me growth-versus-profit has not landed yet and Unit 4 should revisit it.
